title: Rays and Gaps: Almost-All Goldbach Theorems for Consecutive and Shifted Primes
content: For $q = 2^k$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$ let $R_{a,q}(N)=\sum_{p_1+p_2=N,\ p_1\equiv a\ (q)} (\log p_1)(\log p_2)$ be the restricted weighted Goldbach sum, with candidate main term $M_{a,q}(N)=\frac{2C_2}{\varphi(q)}\,\mathfrak{S}(N)\,N$ and exceptional set $\mathcal{E}_{a,q}(X)=\{N\le X \text{ even}: R_{a,q}(N)=0\}$. We first prove, by the circle method with the additive-shift decomposition of the sum over a progression modulo $2^k$, an exact evaluation of the singular series of the progression and the mean-square bound $\sum_{N\le X}\left|R_{a,q}(N)-M_{a,q}(N)\right|^{2}\ll_{A,q} X^{3}(\log X)^{-A}$ for every $A>0$, hence $\#\mathcal{E}_{a,q}(X)\ll_{A,q} X(\log X)^{-A}$. Writing $p_n$ for the $n$-th prime, $g_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$ and $N_n=p_n+p_{n+1}$, we then prove an elementary transfer principle: if $f$ maps a set of indices injectively (or with bounded multiplicity) into the even integers with at most linear growth, the number of indices $n\le X$ with $R_{a,q}(f(n))=0$ is at most a bounded multiple of $\#\mathcal{E}_{a,q}(\kappa X+\lambda)$. The consequences are uniform in the residue class ("ray") of $p_n$ modulo $q$ and cover $N_n=p_n+p_{n+1}$, $p_n+p_{n+k}$ and the shifted primes $p+h$ with $h$ odd; each of these sets of even integers has a restricted Goldbach representation for almost all primes in every ray, with a saving of every power of $\log X$. We record which of the representations are trivial (a summand equal to $p_n$ or $p_{n+1}$). For a modulus $q$ with an odd prime factor $\ell$ we prove that $N_n\equiv a\ (\ell)$ is a condition on the pair of rays of $p_n$ and $p_{n+1}$, that $R_{a,q}(N_n)=O(\log N_n)$ on that set, and, by a theorem of Shiu, that this set is infinite; for $q=3$ we verify that $R_{a,q}(N_n)=0$ if and only if $N_n\equiv 1\ (3)$ and $N_n-3$ is composite. The digit-repulsion bias of Lemke Oliver and Soundararajan is documented on 5,761,451 consecutive pairs below $10^8$, together with the dependence of the mean gap on the ray of origin, a fit of the cumulative admissibility function with closed-form constants, and a comparison of the mod-3 joint frequencies with the Lemke Oliver–Soundararajan prediction at four scales up to $10^9$. Next, the relative second moment of $R_{a,q}(N)-M_{a,q}(N)$ depends on $N$ modulo $q$ through the symmetry $p_1\leftrightarrow p_2$: for $N\equiv 2a\ (q)$ the variance ratio is 2.0 to 2.1 for $q=16,32$ and within two standard errors of 2 for every class tested at $q=8,16,32$. Along $N_n$ this class effect, together with the residues of $N_n$ modulo 3 and 5, predicts the second moment by ray of $p_n$ to within 3% overall, and a recipe fixed in advance at $q=16$ predicts the level, the spread among the eight rays, and the pattern across rays with correlation 0.96. In a temporal split of the primes below $10^8$ the last ray predicts the next ray with accuracy 0.311 against 0.25, while the rays of the past explain at most 0.19% of the variance of the normalised gap. Finally, the amplitude $\mathfrak{S}(p+h)$ of the main term along shifted primes has a limit law given by an explicit random Euler product $Y_h$, with convergence of all moments, an entire moment generating function, a doubly exponentially thin upper tail, and no atoms. Every statement carries an explicit status label. This paper continues [18]: it restates its local-obstruction theorem and strengthens its second-moment estimate to a saving of every power of $\log X$; Section 1.5 records the precise relation.
